questions.q: Match each kind of address to what it identifies.
pairs: A specific piece of hardware, set when it was manufactured
A device's position on a network, which can change
questions.feedback: MAC is permanent and belongs to the hardware; IP is assigned and can change when a device moves network.

questions.q: A laptop is taken from home to school. Which of its addresses changes?
questions.feedback: The MAC address is burnt into the network interface card. The IP address is given out by whichever network the laptop joins.

markPoints.exemplar: The supply of IPv4 addresses was running out.

markPoints.concept: because IPv6 uses many more bits, it provides vastly more addresses
markPoints.exemplar: IPv6 uses 128 bits, which gives vastly more addresses.

questions.example: IPv4 uses 32 bits, which gives about four billion addresses, and with so many devices connecting they were running out. IPv6 uses 128 bits, which provides an enormous number of addresses and removes the problem.
questions.paraphrase: There were simply not enough of the old 32-bit addresses left for all the devices coming online, so a scheme with 128 bits and a far larger supply was introduced.
questions.feedback: Running out, then what IPv6 does about it.

questions.q: How many bits does an IPv4 address use?
questions.feedback: 32 bits, written as four numbers from 0 to 255. 48 bits is a MAC address and 128 is IPv6.
